criterion_notes.c1: Examines piped drinking-water service expansion and service quality in the West Zone of Metro Manila, including connecting unserved households and improving 24-hour supply continuity and pressure.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the paper does not examine any rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement rules, or utility ownership/regulatory rules governing access); instead, the studied intervention is an engineering and operational non-revenue water (NRW) reduction program (DMA hydraulic isolation, leak detection and repair, pressure management, selective pipe replacement, and meter management). Maynilad's 1997 privatization, 2004-2006 government takeover, and 2007 re-privatization are recounted solely as unanalysed macro-governance background, while closing illegal connections and obtaining LGU excavation permits are mentioned only in passing without rule-level analysis. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it also fails (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because creating an internal Central NRW engineering department and executing technical water-loss reduction/CAPEX management is routine operational engineering delivery rather than an empirical examination of a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary utility operational data from Maynilad (water balance and DMA measurements, 1997-2013 annual NRW series in Figure 3, 2007 vs. 2013 water availability and pressure maps in Figures 4-5, and 2007 vs. 2013 performance indicators in Table 1), presented as a descriptive practitioner pre-post operational case report without formal academic research methods.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports piped water service coverage (increasing from 81% in 2007 to 96% in 2013), billed customer services/household connections (increasing from 700,000 to 1,129,000, connecting 430,000 additional households), 24-hour uninterrupted supply availability (47% to 98% of customers), and water pressure >= 7 psi (53% to 100% of customers).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the utility and service population (Maynilad West Zone concession in Metro Manila, ~9.3 million people, 700,000 to 1,129,000 billed accounts), the operational NRW engineering intervention (2008-2013), utility-level access and financial outcomes, and a descriptive pre-post utility operational case report design.

evidence_quotes.quote: The water that was saved in turn was used to supply additional 400,000 new customers in the expansion areas and generally improved the level of service of the existing customers by providing higher water pressure and longer water availability.

The 1997 privatization was in response to the then pressing needs which were (1) poor level of service, (2) high non-revenue water and (3) the need to develop other water sources to meet the growing demand.
Central NRW also has its own Engineering and Construction Department to design and implement projects related to NRW reduction.
Active leakage control (ALC) is the pro-active leakage reduction procedure to identify water loss in the DMA. It involves detection and repair of both detected and reported leaks.

Maynilad’s NRW average NRW volume in 2013 is 768 MLD for an NRW level of 38.7%. This is equivalent to a reduction of 738 MLD from the 2007 NRW volume of 1,506 MLD and a 27% point reduction in NRW level.
In 2013, 100% of Maynilad’s customers were experiencing a minimum of 7 psi water pressure while 98% were getting uninterrupted water supply for 24 hours/day.

raw_response.exposure: Technical and operational Non-Revenue Water (NRW) reduction and management program (2008-2013, USD 280M CAPEX), comprising creation of a dedicated Central NRW engineering team, hydraulic isolation into 138 hydraulic systems and 1,372 district metered areas (DMAs), flow/pressure diagnostics, active leakage control and leak repair, selective pipe replacement, customer meter replacement, and staff training
raw_response.outcome: Piped water service coverage (81% to 96%), billed customer services/connections (700,000 to 1,129,000; 430,000 additional households tapped), 24-hour uninterrupted water supply availability (47% to 98% of customers), minimum 7 psi water pressure (53% to 100% of customers), NRW volume and percentage (66% to 39%), billed volume, and utility revenue
raw_response.population_and_sample: Maynilad Water Services, Inc. West Zone concession area in Metro Manila, Philippines (17 cities and municipalities, approximately 9.3 million population; 700,000 billed customer accounts in 2007 increasing to 1,129,000 in 2013; unit of analysis: utility)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this practitioner utility report documents substantial gains in piped water service coverage (81% to 96%), household connections (+430,000 households), and 24-hour continuity (47% to 98%) for Maynilad in Metro Manila between 2007 and 2013, the studied intervention is an engineering and operational non-revenue water (NRW) reduction program (DMA hydraulic zoning, active leak detection and repair, pressure management, selective pipe replacement, customer meter replacement, and internal engineering team management) alongside CAPEX/revenue considerations. Privatization and concession history (1997, 2004-2006, 2007) are described solely as unanalysed background context, and no legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism governing household service access is empirically examined under either the narrow 2026-10-13 reading or the plain wording of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Descriptive pre-post utility operational case report (2007 vs. 2013)
